goals: Describe simple, glandular and compound epithelia and cell junctions

slides.heading: Structural Organisation in Animals
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the four basic tissues that build every animal organ.

visual.alt: Flow from cells to tissues, organs and organ systems

slides.narration: In multicellular animals, groups of similar cells together with the material between them perform a common function. Such a group is a tissue. Tissues combine to form organs, and organs work together as organ systems, which share the work of the body.

slides.heading: Four basic tissues
slides.body_md: Tissues are grouped by structure and function into four basic types.

rows: Covers surfaces, lines cavities and tubes
Controls the body’s response to change

visual.alt: Table of the four basic animal tissues with roles and examples

slides.narration: Epithelium covers and lines. Connective tissue links and supports. Muscle contracts. And neural tissue controls how the body responds to changing conditions. Every organ, such as the stomach, is built from several of these tissues working together.

slides.heading: Simple epithelium
slides.body_md: Epithelial cells are **compactly packed** with little matrix between them and rest on a **basement membrane**. **Simple** epithelium has **one layer** of cells and lines body cavities, ducts and tubes.

slides.narration: Squamous cells are thin and flat, ideal where substances must diffuse, as in the air sacs of the lungs. Cuboidal cells line gland ducts and kidney tubules, where microvilli help absorption. Columnar cells line the stomach and intestine. Ciliated cells move mucus or particles in one direction.

slides.heading: Glandular epithelium
slides.body_md: Some cuboidal or columnar cells are **specialised for secretion**.

rows: Goblet cells of the alimentary canal
Mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk, digestive enzymes
No ducts; hormones pass into the fluid bathing the gland

visual.alt: Table of kinds of glandular epithelium with examples

slides.narration: A gland may be a single cell, like a goblet cell that releases mucus, or a large cluster of cells, like a salivary gland. Exocrine glands deliver their products through ducts. Endocrine glands have no ducts and release hormones straight into the surrounding fluid.

slides.heading: Compound epithelium and cell junctions
slides.body_md: **Compound** epithelium has **two or more layers**; it **protects** against chemical and mechanical stresses and has little role in secretion or absorption. It covers the **skin** and lines the **buccal cavity, pharynx** and the ducts of salivary glands and pancreas.

rows: Stops substances leaking across a tissue
Connects the cytoplasm of adjoining cells for rapid transfer of ions and small molecules

visual.alt: Table of three cell junctions and their roles

slides.narration: In nearly all animal tissues, special junctions link cells structurally and functionally. Tight junctions seal the gaps. Adhering junctions act like cement. And gap junctions open channels between neighbouring cells so that they can communicate quickly.

slides.heading: Connective tissue
slides.body_md: Connective tissues are the **most abundant** tissues. Except in blood, their cells secrete fibres of **collagen** or **elastin** and modified polysaccharides that form the **matrix**.

slides.narration: Fibres give strength, elasticity and flexibility. In areolar tissue beneath the skin, fibroblasts make fibres, macrophages engulf invaders and mast cells release chemicals. Cartilage has cells inside small cavities in a bendable matrix, while bone has a hard matrix rich in calcium salts.

slides.heading: Types of connective tissue
slides.body_md: Three types are recognised.

rows: Cells and fibres loosely arranged in a semi-fluid ground substance
Areolar tissue beneath the skin; adipose tissue storing fat
Collagen fibres in parallel rows between rows of fibroblasts
Tendons (muscle to bone); ligaments (bone to bone)
Tip of nose and outer ear; limb bones; blood in vessels

visual.alt: Table of loose, dense and specialised connective tissues

slides.narration: Loose tissues pack and cushion organs and store fat. Dense regular tissue, with fibres all in one direction, makes strong tendons and ligaments. Bone supports and protects soft organs, and its marrow makes blood cells. Blood is a fluid connective tissue that carries materials around the body.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how big is the cell?
slides.body_md: A photograph of cuboidal epithelium is taken at a magnification of 400. One cell measures 6 mm on the print. Find its real width in micrometres.
bullets: Real size $= \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}}$.
Convert millimetres to micrometres first: 1 mm = 1000 µm.

visual.alt: Worked table: real width 15 micrometres

slides.narration: Change the image size into micrometres, which gives six thousand. Divide by the magnification of four hundred. The cell is fifteen micrometres wide, a typical size for an epithelial cell.

slides.body_md: Muscle is made of long fibres containing **myofibrils**; fibres contract in response to stimulation and then relax.

slides.narration: Skeletal muscle, attached to bones, is striated and voluntary. Smooth muscle in the walls of the gut and blood vessels has spindle cells without striations and works involuntarily. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart; its branched cells are joined by intercalated discs, so they contract as a unit.

slides.heading: Neural tissue
slides.body_md: **Neurons** are the excitable cells. **Neuroglia** protect and support neurons and make up **more than half the volume** of neural tissue.

slides.narration: When a neuron is suitably stimulated, an electrical disturbance is generated and travels swiftly along its plasma membrane. When it reaches the endings of the axon, it triggers stimulation or inhibition of the next neurons or other cells. Neural tissue exerts the greatest control over the body’s responsiveness.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: naming a tissue from clues
slides.body_md: A student scores 36 cells in one field of a kidney tubule slide: 27 are cube-shaped with round central nuclei and microvilli, and 9 are thin and flat. Name the main tissue and find its share.
bullets: Cube-shaped cells with central nuclei: **cuboidal epithelium**; microvilli suggest the **proximal convoluted tubule**.
Share $= \dfrac{27}{36} \times 100 = 75$ percent.
Thin flat cells nearby are squamous epithelium, as in other parts of the tubule and in capillary walls.

rows: Absorption, as in the proximal tubule

visual.alt: Worked table: 75 percent of cells are cuboidal

slides.narration: Use shape first. Cube-like cells with round central nuclei are cuboidal. Microvilli point to an absorbing surface. Twenty-seven out of thirty-six is three quarters, so seventy-five percent of the cells are cuboidal.

slides.heading: Quick check: muscle
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about cardiac muscle.
slides.narration: Quick check. Do you control your heartbeat at will?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Epithelium: simple (squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated), glandular (exocrine, endocrine) and compound; tight, adhering and gap junctions.
Connective: loose (areolar, adipose), dense (regular: tendons, ligaments; irregular: skin), specialised (cartilage, bone, blood).
Muscle: skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (spindle, involuntary), cardiac (branched, intercalated discs).
Neural: neurons carry impulses; neuroglia protect and support, over half the volume.

visual.alt: Summary table of four tissues and their key roles

slides.narration: To recap: epithelium covers and lines, connective tissue links and supports, muscle contracts and neural tissue controls. Learn one location for each kind, because questions often describe a place and ask you to name the tissue.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **one location** for each epithelium and connective tissue.
Separate **tendon** (muscle to bone) from **ligament** (bone to bone).
Tabulate the **three muscles**: shape, striations, nuclei, control.
Name the **three junctions** with their roles.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Link every tissue to a location. Do not confuse tendons with ligaments. Compare the three muscles in a table. And remember the roles of tight, adhering and gap junctions.

decks.title: Structural Organisation in Animals — Part 2: The frog
goals: Describe the habitat, habits and external features of the frog
Describe its digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems
Describe its excretory, nervous and reproductive systems
Explain the frog’s importance to people and ecosystems

slides.heading: The frog
slides.body_md: Part 2 — morphology and anatomy of the common Indian frog, Rana tigrina.

visual.alt: Flow from habitat to external features, organ systems and reproduction

slides.narration: Frogs live both on land and in fresh water and belong to the class Amphibia of the phylum Chordata. Studying one animal in depth shows how tissues are organised into organs and organ systems that keep it alive.

slides.heading: Habitat and habits
slides.body_md: Frogs are **cold-blooded (poikilotherms)**: their body temperature varies with the surroundings.

rows: Can change colour to hide from enemies (camouflage)
Summer sleep in deep burrows to escape heat
Winter sleep in burrows to escape cold
Never drinks; absorbs water through the skin

visual.alt: Table of habits of the frog

slides.narration: Because they cannot keep a steady body temperature, frogs avoid extreme heat and cold by burrowing deep into the ground, in summer sleep and in winter sleep. They can change colour to blend with their surroundings, and they take in water through their moist skin instead of drinking.

slides.heading: External features
slides.body_md: The body is divided into **head and trunk**; there is **no neck and no tail**. The skin is smooth, slippery and moist with mucus; olive green with dark spots above, pale yellow below.

slides.narration: Above the mouth is a pair of nostrils. The bulging eyes are covered by a nictitating membrane in water, and behind each eye is a tympanum that receives sound. Forelimbs end in four digits; the larger, muscular hind limbs end in five webbed digits that help in swimming, leaping and burrowing.

slides.heading: Quick check: external features
slides.body_md: Which structure protects the eyes of a frog under water?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is a membrane that can be drawn across the eye.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: male or female?
slides.body_md: Two frogs from a pond are examined. Frog X has a swelling on the first digit of each forelimb and inflates a pair of sacs when it croaks; frog Y has neither. Identify the sexes.
bullets: The swelling is a **copulatory pad**; the sacs are **vocal sacs**.
Both are found **only in males**, so **X is male** and **Y is female**.
Such external differences between the sexes are called **sexual dimorphism**.

visual.alt: Worked table: frog X male, frog Y female

slides.narration: Look for two clues. A pad on the first finger helps the male hold the female while mating, and vocal sacs produce the croaking calls. Frog X has both, so it is the male. Frog Y lacks them, so it is the female.

slides.heading: Digestive system
slides.body_md: The alimentary canal is **short** because frogs are **carnivores**. Food is caught by the **bilobed tongue**.

visual.alt: Flow of food through the alimentary canal of the frog

slides.narration: In the stomach, acid and gastric juices turn food into chyme. The duodenum receives bile, stored in the gall bladder, and pancreatic juice through a common bile duct. Bile emulsifies fat, and pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins. Villi and microvilli absorb the products, and waste leaves through the cloaca.

slides.heading: Respiration
slides.body_md: The frog exchanges gases in **water and on land**.

visual.alt: Table of how the frog breathes in different situations

slides.narration: The lungs are a pair of pink, sac-like organs in the upper part of the trunk. Air enters through the nostrils into the buccal cavity and then the lungs. In water, and while buried during summer or winter sleep, the frog relies on its moist skin.

slides.heading: Heart and circulation
slides.body_md: The frog has a **closed** circulation and a **lymphatic system**. The heart has **three chambers** and is covered by a **pericardium**.

Special veins link the liver and intestine in the hepatic portal system, and the kidneys and lower body in the renal portal system. Red blood cells are nucleated and contain haemoglobin.

slides.narration: Quick check. It is a triangular chamber on the dorsal side of the heart.

slides.narration: In the male, testes are attached to the kidneys by the mesorchium. Ten to twelve vasa efferentia enter each kidney and open into Bidder’s canal, which leads to the urinogenital duct and the cloaca. In the female, the ovaries have no link with the kidneys, and the oviducts open into the cloaca separately from the ureters.

slides.heading: Nervous system and sense organs
slides.body_md: Control comes from the **neural system** and **endocrine glands** (pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads). The brain is enclosed in a **cranium**; **ten pairs** of cranial nerves arise from it.

rows: Olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon
Cerebellum and medulla oblongata, which continues as the spinal cord through the foramen magnum

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the frog brain

slides.narration: The nervous system has central, peripheral and autonomic parts. Sense organs include sensory papillae for touch, taste buds, the nasal epithelium for smell, simple eyes, and the tympanum with internal ears. The ear serves for both hearing and balance, and there is no external ear.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from eggs to froglets
slides.body_md: A female lays 2800 eggs. Suppose 60 percent hatch into tadpoles and 5 percent of the tadpoles complete metamorphosis. How many young frogs result?
bullets: Tadpoles $= 2800 \times \dfrac{60}{100} = 1680$.
Froglets $= 1680 \times \dfrac{5}{100} = 84$.
A mature female can lay 2500 to 3000 eggs at a time; large numbers make up for heavy losses.

visual.alt: Worked flow: 84 froglets from 2800 eggs

slides.narration: Apply each survival percentage in turn. Sixty percent of two thousand eight hundred is one thousand six hundred and eighty tadpoles. Five percent of those is eighty-four young frogs. Fertilisation is external and eggs develop in water, so many are lost.

slides.heading: Quick check: brain
slides.body_md: To which part of the frog’s brain do the optic lobes belong?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall which part of the brain is marked by a pair of lobes.

slides.heading: Reproduction and importance
slides.body_md: A pair of **ovaries** lies near the kidneys; **oviducts** open into the cloaca. **Fertilisation is external**, in water; development passes through a **tadpole** larva that undergoes **metamorphosis**.

rows: Important link in food chains and food webs
Muscular legs eaten in some countries

visual.alt: Table of the importance of frogs

slides.narration: Frogs are beneficial to people. By eating insects they protect crops, and as prey and predator they form an important link in food chains and food webs, helping to maintain ecological balance.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Rana tigrina: poikilotherm; camouflage; aestivation and hibernation; absorbs water through skin.
Head and trunk, no neck or tail; nictitating membrane, tympanum; forelimbs four digits, hind limbs five webbed digits; males with vocal sacs and copulatory pads.
Short gut; bile and pancreatic juice via common bile duct; skin, buccal cavity and lungs for respiration.
Three-chambered heart with sinus venosus and conus arteriosus; hepatic and renal portal systems; nucleated RBCs.
Kidneys and cloaca; ureotelic; male urinogenital duct via Bidder’s canal; ten pairs of cranial nerves; external fertilisation; tadpole.

rows: Skin in water; lungs on land

visual.alt: Summary table of frog organ systems

slides.narration: To recap: the frog is a cold-blooded amphibian with a head and trunk, a short carnivore gut, skin and lung breathing, a three-chambered heart, urea excretion and external fertilisation in water followed by a tadpole stage.

bullets: Give **two differences** between male and female frogs.
Trace the **path of blood** through the heart chambers in order.
Contrast the **male and female** routes to the cloaca.
Place each **brain part** with its lobes correctly.

notes.title: Structural Organisation in Animals — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Animal tissues: epithelial and connective
sections.body_md:
A **tissue** is a group of similar cells, together with the intercellular substance, that performs a specific function. Organs are built from tissues and organs work together as organ systems. Animal tissues are of four basic types: **epithelial, connective, muscular and neural**.

**Epithelial tissue** covers body surfaces and lines body cavities, ducts and tubes. Its cells are compactly packed with little intercellular matrix and rest on a **basement membrane**.
- **Simple epithelium** (one layer): **squamous** — a single thin layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries, in the walls of blood vessels and the air sacs of lungs, where diffusion occurs; **cuboidal** — cube-like cells in the ducts of glands and the tubular parts of nephrons, with **microvilli** on the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule; **columnar** — tall, slender cells with nuclei at the base, lining the stomach and intestine, with microvilli for absorption; **ciliated** — cuboidal or columnar cells bearing cilia that move particles or mucus in one direction, in the bronchioles and fallopian tubes.
- **Glandular epithelium**: cuboidal or columnar cells specialised for secretion. **Unicellular** glands are isolated cells such as the **goblet cells** of the alimentary canal; **multicellular** glands are clusters such as the **salivary gland**. **Exocrine** glands secrete mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk and digestive enzymes through ducts; **endocrine** glands have no ducts and release **hormones** directly into the fluid bathing the gland.
- **Compound epithelium** (two or more layers) has a limited role in secretion and absorption; it protects against chemical and mechanical stresses. It covers the dry surface of the **skin** and lines the moist **buccal cavity, pharynx**, the inner lining of the ducts of **salivary glands** and of **pancreatic ducts**.
- **Cell junctions**: **tight junctions** stop substances leaking across a tissue; **adhering junctions** cement neighbouring cells together; **gap junctions** connect the cytoplasm of adjoining cells for rapid transfer of ions, small molecules and sometimes big molecules.

**Connective tissues** are the most abundant and widely distributed tissues; they link and support other tissues. In all except blood, the cells secrete fibres of **collagen** or **elastin**, which give strength, elasticity and flexibility, and modified polysaccharides that form the **matrix** (ground substance).
- **Loose connective tissue**: cells and fibres loosely arranged in a semi-fluid ground substance. **Areolar tissue** beneath the skin supports the epithelium and contains **fibroblasts** (which make fibres), **macrophages** and **mast cells**. **Adipose tissue**, also beneath the skin, stores fats made from nutrients not used immediately.
- **Dense connective tissue**: fibres and fibroblasts compactly packed. **Dense regular**: collagen fibres in parallel rows between rows of fibroblasts — **tendons** attach skeletal muscle to bone and **ligaments** attach bone to bone. **Dense irregular**: fibres oriented in different directions, as in the **skin**.
- **Specialised connective tissue**: **cartilage** — a solid, pliable matrix of chondroitin salts that resists compression, with **chondrocytes** in small cavities (lacunae); found at the tip of the nose, outer ear joints, between adjacent vertebrae and in the limbs and hands of adults. **Bone** — a hard, non-pliable matrix rich in **calcium salts and collagen**, with **osteocytes** in lacunae; it supports and protects soft organs, interacts with muscles for movement, and the **bone marrow** of some bones produces blood cells. **Blood** — a fluid connective tissue of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets, the main circulating fluid that transports substances.

sections.heading: 2. Animal tissues: muscular and neural
sections.body_md:
**Muscle tissue** is made of long, cylindrical fibres arranged in parallel; each fibre contains many fine **myofibrils**. Fibres contract (shorten) in response to stimulation and then relax, in a coordinated way, to move the body and its parts.
- **Skeletal muscle**: closely attached to skeletal bones; fibres are **striated**, unbranched and **multinucleate**, bundled together in parallel; **voluntary** (for example the biceps).
- **Smooth muscle**: fibres **taper at both ends** (fusiform) and show **no striations**; cell junctions hold them together in bundles; found in the walls of **blood vessels, stomach and intestine**; **involuntary**.
- **Cardiac muscle**: the contractile tissue found **only in the heart**; striated and branched; cell junctions fuse the plasma membranes of cardiac cells, and **communication junctions (intercalated discs)** at some fusion points allow the cells to **contract as a unit**; involuntary.

**Neural tissue** exerts the greatest control over the body’s responsiveness to changing conditions. **Neurons**, the unit of the neural system, are excitable cells. **Neuroglial cells** protect and support neurons and make up **more than half the volume** of neural tissue in our body. When a neuron is suitably stimulated, an electrical disturbance is generated which travels swiftly along its plasma membrane; its arrival at the neuron’s endings (axon terminals) triggers stimulation or inhibition of adjacent neurons and other cells.

sections.heading: 3. The frog: morphology
sections.body_md:
The common Indian frog is ***Rana tigrina***. Frogs live on land and in fresh water and belong to the class **Amphibia** of phylum Chordata.

**Habits.** Frogs are **cold-blooded (poikilotherms)**: their body temperature varies with the environment. They can **change colour** to hide from enemies (**camouflage**). They take shelter in deep burrows to protect themselves from extreme heat in summer (**aestivation**, summer sleep) and from extreme cold in winter (**hibernation**, winter sleep).

**External features.** The skin is smooth and slippery because of mucus and is always moist. The dorsal side is olive green with dark irregular spots; the ventral side is uniformly pale yellow. The frog **never drinks water** but absorbs it through the skin. The body is divided into **head and trunk**; a **neck and tail are absent**. Above the mouth is a pair of **nostrils**. The **eyes** are bulged and covered by a **nictitating membrane** that protects them while in water. On either side of the eyes a membranous **tympanum** (ear) receives sound signals. **Forelimbs** end in **four digits**; **hind limbs**, larger and more muscular, end in **five digits**, and the feet have **webbed digits** that help in swimming. Limbs are used for swimming, walking, leaping and burrowing.

**Sexual dimorphism.** Male frogs have sound-producing **vocal sacs** and a **copulatory pad** on the first digit of each forelimb; these are absent in females.

key_terms.definition_md: An animal whose body temperature varies with its surroundings.
Summer sleep: inactivity in burrows to escape heat and drought.
Winter sleep: inactivity in burrows to escape cold.
A membrane that covers and protects the frog’s eye in water.

sections.heading: 4. The frog: anatomy
sections.body_md:
**Digestive system.** The alimentary canal is **short** because frogs are **carnivores**, so the intestine is reduced. Mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → intestine → rectum → **cloaca**. The **liver** secretes bile, stored in the **gall bladder**; the **pancreas** produces pancreatic juice with digestive enzymes. Food is captured by the **bilobed tongue**. In the stomach, **HCl and gastric juices** digest food; the partly digested food, **chyme**, passes to the **duodenum**, which receives bile and pancreatic juice through a **common bile duct**. Bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins. Final digestion occurs in the intestine, and the products are absorbed by **villi and microvilli**. Undigested waste passes out through the cloaca.

**Respiration.** In water, the skin acts as the respiratory organ (**cutaneous respiration**): dissolved oxygen is exchanged by diffusion. On land, the **buccal cavity, skin and lungs** serve; the lungs are a pair of elongated, pink, sac-like structures in the upper trunk (thorax), and air enters through the nostrils into the buccal cavity and then the lungs (**pulmonary respiration**). During aestivation and hibernation, gas exchange occurs through the skin.

**Circulation.** The blood vascular system is **closed**; there is also a **lymphatic system** of lymph, lymph channels and lymph nodes. The **heart** is muscular, **three-chambered** (two atria, one ventricle), lies in the upper body cavity and is covered by a **pericardium**. A triangular **sinus venosus** joins the right atrium and receives blood through the **venae cavae**. The ventricle opens into a sac-like **conus arteriosus** on the ventral side. Arteries carry blood away from the heart (arterial system) and veins bring it back (venous system). The **hepatic portal system** links the liver and intestine; the **renal portal system** links the kidneys and the lower body. Blood has plasma and cells — **red blood cells (nucleated, with haemoglobin)**, white blood cells and platelets. **Lymph** lacks a few proteins and red blood cells. Blood carries nutrients, gases and water.

**Excretion.** A pair of **kidneys**, ureters, the cloaca and the **urinary bladder**. The kidneys are compact, dark red and bean-like, a little posterior in the body cavity on either side of the vertebral column; each is made of many **uriniferous tubules (nephrons)**. In the **male**, the ureters act as **urinogenital ducts** opening into the cloaca; in the **female**, the ureters and oviducts open **separately** into the cloaca. The thin-walled bladder lies ventral to the rectum and opens into the cloaca. The frog excretes **urea** and is **ureotelic**.

**Control and coordination.** Endocrine glands: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads. The nervous system has a **central** part (brain and spinal cord), a **peripheral** part (cranial and spinal nerves) and an **autonomic** part (sympathetic and parasympathetic). **Ten pairs of cranial nerves** arise from the brain, which is enclosed in the **cranium**. **Forebrain**: olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon; **midbrain**: a pair of **optic lobes**; **hindbrain**: cerebellum and **medulla oblongata**, which passes through the **foramen magnum** and continues into the spinal cord in the vertebral column. Sense organs: sensory papillae (touch), taste buds, nasal epithelium (smell), eyes (vision) and tympanum with internal ears (hearing); the eyes and internal ears are well organised, the rest are cellular aggregations around nerve endings. The eyes are a pair of spherical **simple eyes** in the orbits. There is **no external ear**; the ear serves for **hearing and balance**.

**Reproduction.** Male: a pair of yellowish, ovoid **testes** attached to the upper part of the kidneys by a double fold of peritoneum, the **mesorchium**; **10–12 vasa efferentia** from each testis enter the kidney and open into **Bidder’s canal**, which communicates with the urinogenital duct opening into the cloaca. The **cloaca** is a small median chamber that passes faecal matter, urine and sperms to the outside. Female: a pair of **ovaries** near the kidneys with **no functional connection** to them; a pair of **oviducts** opens separately into the cloaca. A mature female can lay **2500–3000 ova** at a time. **Fertilisation is external**, in water; development involves a larval stage, the **tadpole**, which undergoes **metamorphosis** into the adult.

**Importance.** Frogs eat insects and protect crops; they maintain ecological balance as an important link in food chains and food webs; their muscular legs are eaten in some countries.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling a tendon a ligament (tendon: muscle to bone; ligament: bone to bone).
- Saying endocrine glands have ducts.
- Describing cardiac muscle as voluntary or unstriated.
- Giving the frog a neck, a tail or an external ear.
- Saying frog red blood cells have no nucleus.
- Mixing up aestivation (summer) and hibernation (winter).
- Writing that the female frog has a urinogenital duct (the ureters and oviducts open separately).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name a tissue from its location, a junction, a frog structure or a brain part.
- 2–3-mark answers: compare exocrine and endocrine glands; tendons and ligaments; three muscles; digestion or respiration in the frog; path of blood through the heart.
- 5-mark answers: epithelial or connective tissues with examples; two organ systems of the frog; evaluation of the frog’s adaptations.
- Case-based items: identifying tissues from slides, an injury, a pond survey or a dissection model, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: A slide shows a single layer of thin, flat cells with irregular boundaries, taken from the wall of a lung air sac. The tissue is
questions.solution_md: One layer of thin, flat cells forming a diffusion boundary is squamous epithelium — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule of a nephron are cube-shaped and carry microvilli on their free surface. Which tissue is this, and what do the microvilli do?

options.text_md: Squamous epithelium; they sweep mucus along
Columnar epithelium; they release hormones into blood
Cuboidal epithelium; they increase the surface area for absorption

questions.solution_md: Cube-like cells are cuboidal epithelium; microvilli enlarge the absorbing surface — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The mucus-secreting goblet cells scattered in the lining of the alimentary canal are an example of
questions.solution_md: Each goblet cell is a single secretory cell: a unicellular gland — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Dust trapped in mucus is moved steadily upwards along the inner surface of the bronchioles. Which tissue lines this surface?
questions.solution_md: Beating cilia move particles or mucus in a specific direction over the epithelium — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these surfaces is covered by compound epithelium?

options.text_md: The air sacs of the lungs
The inner lining of the intestine
The moist lining of the buccal cavity and pharynx

questions.solution_md: Compound (many-layered) epithelium covers the skin and lines the buccal cavity, pharynx and ducts of salivary glands and pancreas — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which junction between epithelial cells stops substances from leaking across the tissue?
questions.solution_md: Tight junctions seal neighbouring cells so substances cannot leak between them — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A dye injected into one cell of a tissue is soon seen in the cytoplasm of its neighbours, although no dye leaks out of the tissue. Which junctions allow the passage between cells?
questions.solution_md: Gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of adjoining cells for rapid transfer of ions and small molecules — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A sprinter tears the cord that attaches her calf muscle to the heel bone. The cord is made of
questions.solution_md: A tendon joins skeletal muscle to bone; its collagen fibres lie in parallel rows, so it is dense regular tissue — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The tip of your nose and the outer ear can be bent with a finger and spring back into shape. The supporting tissue is

options.text_md: cartilage, with chondrocytes in small cavities in a pliable matrix
bone, with a matrix rich in calcium salts
dense regular tissue that forms tendons

questions.solution_md: Cartilage has a solid but pliable matrix that resists compression — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Why is blood classed as a connective tissue?

options.text_md: It is a fluid connective tissue: cells move in a fluid matrix, plasma, and it links all parts of the body
It covers the surfaces of organs
It contracts to move the body

questions.solution_md: Blood is a specialised, fluid connective tissue with plasma as matrix and red cells, white cells and platelets — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Nutrients not used at once are converted into fats and stored in
questions.solution_md: Adipose tissue, a loose connective tissue beneath the skin, is specialised to store fats — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A muscle cell is spindle-shaped, tapers at both ends, shows no striations and contracts without conscious control. Where is it most likely to come from?

options.text_md: A muscle attached to the thigh bone

questions.solution_md: Smooth (involuntary) muscle lines the walls of the gut and blood vessels — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Cardiac muscle cells contract as a unit because

options.text_md: communication junctions (intercalated discs) where their membranes fuse let them work together

questions.solution_md: Intercalated discs at the fusion points let cardiac cells contract as one — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about neuroglia is correct?

options.text_md: They make up more than half the volume of neural tissue and protect and support neurons.
They are the excitable cells that carry impulses.
They form less than a tenth of neural tissue.
They are found only in muscle.

questions.solution_md: Neuroglial cells protect and support neurons and occupy more than half the volume of neural tissue — option (a).

Fat-filled cells beneath the skin: adipose tissue

questions.solution_md: False. Endocrine glands have no ducts; hormones pass directly into the fluid bathing the gland. Exocrine glands use ducts.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between exocrine and endocrine glands, naming two products of exocrine glands.

answer.model_answer_md: **Exocrine glands** release their secretions through **ducts** or tubes, for example **mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk** and **digestive enzymes**. **Endocrine glands** have **no ducts**; their products, **hormones**, pass directly into the fluid bathing the gland.

questions.stem_md: One athlete strains a tendon while another sprains a ligament. Compare the two structures in their tissue type and in what they join.

answer.model_answer_md: Both are **dense regular connective tissue**, with **collagen fibres in parallel rows** between rows of fibroblasts, which makes them strong. A **tendon** attaches **skeletal muscle to bone**, while a **ligament** attaches **one bone to another bone**.

questions.solution_md: Same tissue; different attachments.

questions.stem_md: Why are the air sacs of the lungs lined by simple squamous epithelium rather than by compound epithelium?

answer.model_answer_md: Gases must **diffuse quickly** between air and blood. A **single layer of thin, flat cells** gives a very **short diffusion path**. Compound epithelium has **many layers**, which suits **protection** against wear but would slow exchange.

questions.solution_md: Thin barrier for diffusion.

marking_scheme.step: Thin single layer: short diffusion path

questions.stem_md: Name the three kinds of cell junctions found between epithelial and other cells, and state the role of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Tight junctions** seal neighbouring cells together and **stop substances from leaking** across the tissue.

**Adhering junctions** act as **cement**, holding neighbouring cells firmly together.

**Gap junctions** connect the **cytoplasm of adjoining cells**, allowing rapid transfer of **ions, small molecules** and sometimes big molecules, so the cells can **communicate**.

questions.solution_md: Three junctions with roles.

questions.stem_md: Connective tissues are classed into three types. Name them and give two examples of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Loose connective tissue:** cells and fibres loosely arranged in a semi-fluid ground substance — **areolar tissue** beneath the skin and **adipose tissue**, which stores fat.

**Dense connective tissue:** fibres and fibroblasts compactly packed — **tendons and ligaments** (dense regular) and the **skin** (dense irregular).

**Specialised connective tissue:** **cartilage**, **bone** and **blood**.

questions.solution_md: Three types with examples.

questions.stem_md: A slide box contains three unlabelled muscle samples. Explain how shape of fibres, striations and branching would let you sort them into skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Skeletal:** long, **cylindrical, unbranched** fibres with **striations** and many nuclei; it is voluntary, as in the biceps.

**Smooth:** **spindle-shaped** cells that taper at both ends, **no striations**, one central nucleus; it lines the gut and blood vessels.

**Cardiac:** **striated** fibres that are **branched** and joined end to end by **intercalated discs**, found only in the heart.

questions.solution_md: Shape, striations and branching for each.

questions.stem_md: Describe the types of simple epithelium with one location of each, explain glandular epithelium, and state where compound epithelium is found and what it does.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Epithelium** covers body surfaces and lines cavities, ducts and tubes; its cells are packed with little intercellular matrix and rest on a basement membrane.

**Simple epithelium** has one layer of cells. **Squamous** epithelium is a single thin layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries; it forms the walls of blood vessels and the air sacs of the lungs and is suited to diffusion. **Cuboidal** epithelium has cube-like cells; it lines the ducts of glands and the tubular parts of nephrons, where the cells of the proximal tubule bear microvilli for absorption. **Columnar** epithelium has tall, slender cells with nuclei near the base; it lines the stomach and intestine, where microvilli aid absorption. **Ciliated** epithelium has cilia on its free surface that move particles or mucus in one direction, as in the bronchioles and fallopian tubes.

**Glandular epithelium** is made of cuboidal or columnar cells specialised for secretion. It may be **unicellular**, like goblet cells of the gut, or **multicellular**, like salivary glands. **Exocrine** glands secrete mucus, saliva, earwax, oil, milk or enzymes through ducts; **endocrine** glands release hormones directly into the fluid bathing them.

**Compound epithelium** has two or more layers. It covers the dry surface of the skin and lines the buccal cavity, pharynx and the ducts of salivary glands and pancreas. It protects against chemical and mechanical stresses and has little role in secretion or absorption.

questions.solution_md: Simple types, glands, compound.

questions.stem_md: Describe the general features of connective tissue and explain its loose, dense and specialised types, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Connective tissues** are the most abundant and widely distributed tissues; they link and support other tissues. Except in blood, their cells secrete fibres of the structural proteins **collagen** or **elastin**, which give strength, elasticity and flexibility, and also secrete modified polysaccharides that build the **matrix** (ground substance).

**Loose connective tissue** has cells and fibres loosely arranged in a semi-fluid ground substance. **Areolar tissue**, beneath the skin, holds fibroblasts, macrophages and mast cells and supports the epithelium. **Adipose tissue**, also beneath the skin, stores fats.

**Dense connective tissue** has fibres and fibroblasts packed tightly. In **dense regular** tissue the collagen fibres run in parallel bundles, as in **tendons**, which attach muscle to bone, and **ligaments**, which join bone to bone. In **dense irregular** tissue the fibres run in many directions, as in the **skin**.

**Specialised connective tissue** includes **cartilage**, with chondrocytes in lacunae in a pliable matrix (tip of nose, outer ear, between vertebrae); **bone**, a hard matrix rich in calcium salts and collagen with osteocytes in lacunae, whose marrow forms blood cells; and **blood**, a fluid connective tissue of plasma, red cells, white cells and platelets.

questions.solution_md: Features; three types with examples.

questions.stem_md: A frog catches an insect with its tongue. Trace how the insect is digested and absorbed, and how the waste leaves the body.

In the **duodenum**, **bile** (from the gall bladder) emulsifies fat and **pancreatic juice** digests carbohydrates and proteins; both arrive through the **common bile duct**. Final digestion occurs in the **intestine**, and **villi and microvilli** absorb the products. Undigested waste passes to the **rectum** and out through the **cloaca**.

questions.stem_md: Using the structure of its heart, trace the path of blood returning from the body of a frog until it leaves the heart again.

answer.model_answer_md: The frog heart lies in the upper body cavity inside a **pericardium** and has **three chambers**: two **atria** and one **ventricle**. Blood from the body returns through the **venae cavae** into the **sinus venosus**, a triangular chamber on the dorsal side, which opens into the **right atrium**. From the atria blood passes into the single **ventricle**, which pumps it into the **conus arteriosus** on the ventral side, and from there into the **arteries**.

In the **male**, the **ureters** from the kidneys act as **urinogenital ducts**: sperms travel from the testes through **vasa efferentia** into the kidney and **Bidder’s canal**, then share the duct with **urine** to the **cloaca**.

In the **female**, the **ovaries** have **no functional connection** with the kidneys; the **ureters** carry urine and the **oviducts** carry eggs, and they **open separately** into the cloaca.

In both, the **urinary bladder** opens into the cloaca.

questions.stem_md: Describe the digestive and respiratory systems of the frog.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Digestive system.** The alimentary canal is **short**, because the frog is **carnivorous** and its intestine is reduced. The **mouth** opens into the **buccal cavity**, which leads through the **pharynx** and **oesophagus** to the **stomach**, then to the **intestine**, **rectum** and **cloaca**. Food is caught with the **bilobed tongue**. In the stomach, **HCl and gastric juices** act on it, and the partly digested food, **chyme**, passes into the **duodenum**. The duodenum receives **bile** from the **gall bladder**, where the liver’s secretion is stored, and **pancreatic juice** from the **pancreas** through a **common bile duct**. Bile **emulsifies fat**, and pancreatic juice digests **carbohydrates and proteins**. Digestion is completed in the intestine, and the products are absorbed by finger-like **villi and microvilli** on its inner wall. Undigested waste passes into the rectum and out through the cloaca.

**Respiratory system.** In **water**, the moist **skin** is the respiratory surface: dissolved oxygen is exchanged by **diffusion** (cutaneous respiration). On **land**, the **buccal cavity, skin and lungs** all serve. The **lungs** are a pair of elongated, **pink, sac-like** organs in the upper trunk (thorax); air enters through the **nostrils** into the buccal cavity and then the lungs (pulmonary respiration). During **aestivation and hibernation**, gas exchange takes place only through the skin.

questions.solution_md: Digestion and respiration.

marking_scheme.step: Stomach and duodenum: juices via common bile duct
Respiration in water, on land, in dormancy

questions.stem_md: Describe the circulatory and excretory systems of the frog.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Circulation.** The frog has a well-developed **closed** blood vascular system, and also a **lymphatic system** of lymph, lymph channels and lymph nodes. The **heart** is muscular and **three-chambered** (two atria, one ventricle), lies in the upper body cavity and is covered by a **pericardium**. A triangular **sinus venosus** joins the right atrium and receives blood from the **venae cavae**. The ventricle opens into a sac-like **conus arteriosus** on the ventral side. **Arteries** carry blood from the heart to the body and **veins** bring it back. Special venous connections link the **liver and intestine** (hepatic portal system) and the **kidneys and the lower body** (renal portal system). Blood has **plasma** and cells: **nucleated red cells** with haemoglobin, white cells and platelets. Lymph lacks a few proteins and red cells.

**Excretion.** The system consists of a pair of **kidneys**, **ureters**, the **cloaca** and a **urinary bladder**. The kidneys are compact, **dark red and bean-like**, lying on either side of the vertebral column; each is made of many **uriniferous tubules (nephrons)**. In the male, the ureters act as **urinogenital ducts**; in the female, the ureters and oviducts open separately into the cloaca. The thin-walled bladder lies ventral to the rectum and opens into the cloaca. The frog excretes **urea**, so it is **ureotelic**.

questions.solution_md: Heart, vessels, blood; kidneys and ducts.

questions.stem_md: A student says that the frog is “fully adapted to life on land”. Evaluate this claim using the frog’s skin, respiration, limbs, excretion and reproduction.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Features that suit land.** The frog has **lungs** for pulmonary respiration on land, with air entering through the nostrils. Its strong, muscular **hind limbs** allow **walking, leaping and burrowing**, and burrowing lets it survive extreme heat and cold by **aestivation and hibernation**. It excretes **urea** (ureotelic), which is less toxic than ammonia and needs less water to remove than ammonia would.

**Features that tie it to water.** Its **skin** must stay **moist**: it absorbs water through the skin (frogs do not drink) and depends on the skin for gas exchange, so it would dry out in a dry place. In water, the **skin is the only respiratory organ**. Its **webbed hind feet** are adaptations for **swimming**, and the **nictitating membrane** protects the eyes under water. Most importantly, **fertilisation is external and takes place in water**, and the eggs hatch into **aquatic tadpoles**, which must undergo **metamorphosis** before they can live on land.

**Judgement.** The claim is **not justified**. The frog shows several land adaptations, but its moist, permeable skin, its dependence on cutaneous respiration and, above all, its water-bound reproduction and larval stage show that it is an **amphibian**, living a double life on land and in water.

questions.solution_md: Land features, water features, judgement.

marking_scheme.step: Land adaptations: lungs, limbs, burrowing, urea
Water dependence: skin, webbed feet, membrane
